job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Nora Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior customer adviser at a savings bank in Reutlingen. I help people with accounts, small loans and pensions, mostly face to face. I studied finance in Stuttgart, I share a flat with a friend, and I'm engaged to Lukas, who teaches at a primary school. We marry next summer. I sing in the church choir on Thursdays, and on Sundays I have lunch at my parents' house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, customers still need someone who explains a mortgage patiently. To friends I'd say I'm not surprised. Online I'd post nothing, but at choir I'd say it over coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm glad. I use an AI tool sometimes to draft customer emails, and it helps when I'm stuck. But the heart of my job, sitting with an older couple and their savings, is something people want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, finish my banking qualification, and save four hundred a month for the wedding next summer and then a flat. I'd also keep helping at the church fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I know it won't always be easy, but I'm settled in my work and my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a customer you remember.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Keller, eighty-one, came in with a shoebox of old savings books. She wanted to give her grandson money for driving lessons without paying tax. We sat for an hour. I explained the allowance, filled in the form and she brought me a jar of plums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The branches closing. Ours lost two in the district last year. If they close mine, I'd drive forty minutes. That's not AI, it's money, and it's been happening for years.

say: I'd tell colleagues customers still need someone to explain a **mortgage** patiently.
I'd tell friends over coffee after choir that I'm not surprised.
think: I'm glad; the AI tool helps with **emails**, but the heart of the job is people.
Branch closures were a worry long before AI.
do: Save about **£400 a month** for the wedding and a flat.
Keep helping at the church fair.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with the branch closures at the back of my mind.

fieldNote: Sees **patient explanation** to older customers as the product.

Mixes work and **community**: church fair, choir, customers who bring plums.

steps.text: Finish my banking qualification
Save about 400 pounds a month for the wedding and a flat
Keep advising older customers face to face at the branch
Plan the wedding for next summer on a fixed budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use the tools for routine questions and keep advisers for the hard conversations. To friends I'd say it's good for efficiency, as long as people aren't dropped. At church I'd say pray for the young ones starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the chatbot takes the easy questions: balances, cards, standing orders. That's where I start my day. If those calls vanish, my team of five needs fewer people, and the youngest, me, is the obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new tools properly and ask my manager Herr Brandt to put me on the advice desk for mortgages and pensions. I'd stay with the qualification. And I'd keep the wedding savings untouched, because the wedding is the one fixed thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like order, and this is a lot of change at once. But I'd rather face it with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who is afraid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mrs Albrecht, who's been here thirty years, that customers prefer her calm voice to any bot. And I'd offer to sit with her on the new tool. She helped me in my first week, so it's the least I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your fiancé say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas is a teacher, so he's less worried. He says schools will change too, but pupils still need an adult in the room. He tells me to keep the date and trust my work. Some days that's enough.

say: I'd say use the tools for **routine questions** and keep advisers for hard talks.
I'd tell friends it's fine if **people aren't dropped**.
think: The chatbot takes the easy calls where I start my day, so my team may need **fewer people**.
As the youngest I'm the obvious one to go.
do: Learn the new tools properly and ask Herr Brandt for the **advice desk**.
feel: **Uneasy**; I like order and this is a lot of change at once.

fieldNote: Wants to move to the **advice desk**, where a person is still needed.

steps.text: Learn the bank's new chat tools properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need honest talks about what the bank does with its people. To friends I'd say we must look after one another, which is what community is for. At church I'd ask for prayers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my wedding, my flat and my job all depend on the same bank in the next few years, and I can't tell if it would still need advisers. Two years is too short to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding but make it smaller, and put every spare euro in savings, about six hundred a month. I'd ask my father whether his workshop could use my bookkeeping, since I've done it before. And I'd use the AI tools to be faster than anyone else on my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd keep a calm face for customers, but it would sit in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a smaller wedding mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means fewer guests, a simpler meal and a church service that's the same either way. My mother wanted eighty guests. I'd say sixty is fine. A wedding doesn't need a big budget to be a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to learn something new while still earning. With five years I could train as a pensions adviser. With two, I'd be hanging on to what I have and hoping the bank keeps its promises.

say: I'd say the bank needs **honest talks** about what it does with its people.
I'd tell friends we must look after one another, and ask for prayers.
think: My wedding, flat and job all rest on **one bank**, and I can't tell if it would need advisers.
Two years is too short to get ready.
do: Make the wedding **smaller** and save about **£600** a month.
Ask my father about **bookkeeping** at his workshop.
Use the AI tools to be fastest on my team.
feel: **Anxious**; a calm face for customers, but it sits in my stomach.
S2.quote: A wedding doesn't need a big budget to be a wedding.
fieldNote: Protects the **wedding date** but not its size.
Turns to her **father's workshop** and church before the bank.
Learning the tools becomes a way to keep her job, not a hobby.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding guest list from eighty to sixty
Save about 600 euros a month
Ask my father if his workshop needs bookkeeping help
Use the AI tools to be fastest on my team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to retrain advisers properly. To friends I'd say it's a time to build our own safety nets, like families and neighbours. At church I'd say keep the faith and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I could be fine if I move into the human side of the bank. But I'd need to be known as the one customers ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the pensions and family-planning specialist at our branch, get the extra certificate, and keep saving. I'd marry next summer as planned and perhaps start a family in three years. I'd also learn the tools bit by bit, because older customers still need someone to explain them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I think of my grandmother, who said every generation has its storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order of things. In two years I'd shrink the wedding and save everything. In five, I can marry, save and train, one after the other. I'd want the children too, before things get strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your bank itself shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd move to another bank, or the town council, or a pension fund. There are many places that need people who can explain money. I'd also have my family's workshop as a plan Z.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **retrain advisers** properly.
I'd tell friends to build safety nets from family and neighbours.
think: I can be fine if I move into the **human side** of the bank.
I need to be the one customers ask for by name.
do: Become the **pensions specialist** and get the extra certificate.
Marry next summer and plan a **family** within three years.
Learn the tools bit by bit.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**; every generation has its storm.
S3.quote: In two years I'd shrink the wedding and save everything. In five, I can marry, save and train, one after the other.
fieldNote: Longer timeline lets her **keep the order**: marry, save, train.
Plans to be the **specialist** customers ask for.
Has several fallbacks: another bank, the council, a pension fund, the workshop.

steps.text: Become the branch's pensions and family-planning specialist
Get the extra pensions certificate

Learn the new tools bit by bit to explain them to customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's keep our people and teach them. To friends I'd say get on with life. At church I'd say thank you for the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I'll be thirty-two, married, probably with two children, still at the bank or somewhere like it. I'd feel prepared and slightly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry next summer, buy a small flat with Lukas, and work part time when the children come. I'd learn the AI tools as they mature and keep my certificate up to date. And I'd put a little into an index fund every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is enough to raise a child to school age and still be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be honest, kind and hard-working, and to learn to talk to people. The machine can add up. It can't sit with someone who has lost a husband and needs help with the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a few big companies would own everything, and small places like my father's workshop would be squeezed out. I'd like families and small businesses to stay at the centre. I'd vote for local business.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so let's keep our people and teach them.
I'd tell friends to get on with life.
think: I'd be thirty-two, **married** and probably with two children, feeling prepared.
I'm slightly curious about the tools, and not afraid of what comes.
do: Marry next summer and buy a **small flat** with Lukas.
Work **part time** when the children come.
Keep my certificate up to date and learn the tools as they mature.
feel: **Calm**; ten years is enough to raise a child to school age and still be ready.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short for me to marry, save and train, one after the other. Time to train while I'm still earning would help, and banks that keep real people on the counter. And some help for families caught in the middle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of change itself. I'm afraid of change that arrives before people have had a chance to plan.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change itself. I'm afraid of change that arrives before people have had a chance to plan.
portrait: Nora is a **22-year-old customer adviser** at a savings bank in Reutlingen, top of her class, with no debt and family backing.
She uses AI **now and then**, and trusts it once her colleagues do.
She is traditional on **faith, family and community**, and blames branch closures more than software.
Her mood is **uneasy to anxious**, with the wedding date as her fixed point.
She plans in order: **marry, save, train**, with her father's workshop as a fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because two years breaks the order of marrying, saving and training.
whatWouldHelp: **Banks that keep** real people on the counter.
